title: Is there a shorter way to write down the three measurements?
description: The three measured cases of the points X and Y are written as the rows of a table with three columns. Keeko's doubt is that five millimetres can be written as five centimetres.
teaching_notes: One idea: a table with a column for each changing quantity records many cases in a short form, and every entry keeps its unit. Watch for students who write a millimetre reading in the centimetre place without changing the unit.

source: Is there a shorthand way of writing it down? In all the sent
video_script.why: A learner records the three measured cases of X and Y as rows of a table.
video_script.substitution: the book's own three cases of the points X and Y, written as rows of its table
video_script.anchor: a table with three columns that fills row by row, beside the rectangle with its points X and Y
video_script.wrong_answer: five millimetres can be written as five centimetres
video_script.wrong_move: writes the five of five millimetres in the table as five centimetres, so the unit changes without the number changing
video_script.payoff_line: The table holds all three cases in three short rows.

final_answer.value: Rows: (5 mm, 3 cm, 7.4 cm), (1 cm, 1 cm, 7 cm), (2 cm, 4 cm, 7.3 cm)
final_answer.spoken: seven point four, seven, and seven point three centimetres

maths_rules: three columns: distance of X from A, distance of Y from B, length XY
5 mm is half of 1 cm, so the unit stays with the number
video_script.design: A table is built column by column, then filled row by row, with each entry carrying its unit.

beats.on_screen: title card, then three long sentences about the positions of X and Y, one under the other

marks.ask: the three sentences appear one under the other, with their repeated words glowing

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about the three cases we measured.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Each case was written as a long sentence, and the sentences repeated the same words.
Is there a shorter way to write all three down?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

beats.on_screen: the three sentences with only the changing parts highlighted

marks.change: only the changing parts of each sentence glow
marks.cols: the three glowing parts line up as three columns
marks.table: the empty table with its rows appears

narration: <bookmark mark='change'/>In every sentence, only three things change.
<bookmark mark='cols'/>The first is how far ex is from eigh. The second is how far why is from bee. The third is the length ex why.
<bookmark mark='table'/>A table can keep these three things in three columns, with one row for each case.

beats.on_screen: Given: the three cases measured before
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the three cases that we measured with the ruler.

beats.on_screen: To find: the three cases written as rows of a table

marks.find: the task is written under the given line

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to write the three cases as rows of a table.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: columns: X from A | Y from B | length XY

marks.cols: the table with three column headings is drawn

narration: <bookmark mark='cols'/>Step one, make three columns. The first two hold the distances of ex and why, and the third holds the length.

marks.row1: the first row is written with a unit beside every number

narration: <bookmark mark='row1'/>Step two, write case one as a row: five millimetres, three centimetres, and seven point four centimetres.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: row 2: 1 cm | 1 cm | 7 cm; row 3: 2 cm | 4 cm | 7.3 cm
narration: <bookmark mark='row2'/>Step three, write the other two rows. Row two is one centimetre, one centimetre, and seven centimetres.
<bookmark mark='row3'/>Row three is two centimetres, four centimetres, and seven point three centimetres.

beats.on_screen: Answer: three rows: (5 mm, 3 cm, 7.4 cm), (1 cm, 1 cm, 7 cm), (2 cm, 4 cm, 7.3 cm)
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The table holds all three cases in three short rows.
<bookmark mark='res'/>The lengths of ex why are seven point four, seven, and seven point three centimetres.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the table
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: a ruler showing 5 mm as half of 1 cm; the entry 5 cm in the first cell is struck out and 5 mm is restored

marks.doubt: the first cell is changed to 5 cm
marks.fix: a ruler shows 5 mm covering only half of one centimetre
marks.keep: 5 mm is restored and a unit sits beside every number

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks five millimetres can be written as five centimetres.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But five millimetres is only half of one centimetre.
<bookmark mark='keep'/>We write the unit with every number, so millimetres and centimetres are never mixed up.
